name: Rejang
confidence_why: 4 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: McGinn, Richard. 2003. Raising of PMP *a in Bukar-Sadong Land Dayak and Rejang. In John Lynch (ed.), Issues in Austronesian historical phonology, 37-64. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics (PL-550). DOI:10.15144/PL-550.37 (ANU open repository PDF, text).
catalog_locator: section 2.3 'Pre-Rejang word stress', p.40 (p.4); also p.37 item (1) and p.44
catalog_quote: 2.3 Pre-Rejang word stress ... 'Appropriate' in this context means that pre-Rejang's stress system was virtually identical to that of contemporary Malay: stress was final when the penult was *e, otherwise penultimate. ... Nowadays, however, in all contemporary Rejang dialects the stress falls uniformly upon the final syllable of the word. To account for the contemporary data, McGinn (1997) assumed that by the time of Proto Rejang the stress had shifted, so that diphthongisation and other changes affected (newly) stressed schwas from PMP *a, whereas 'root harmonisation' affected (newly) destressed reflexes of *a. [p.37:] (1) CV:CV(C) > CVCV:(C) (both Sadong and Rejang are 'oxytone' languages) [p.44:] Another assumption is that all contemporary Bukar-Sadong dialects have ultimate stress, again like Rejang; certainly, all those which have been investigated show this pattern.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all three quoted passages of McGinn 2003 are verbatim in the text we hold layer at the stated places (p.40 sect. 2.3 line 166; p.37 item (1); p.44). (2) The deciding source is a 2003 historical-phonology paper whose synchronic statement is an aside, but it is by the language's principal modern fieldworker, and three further sources downloaded now agree: McGinn 2005 (Oceanic Linguistics 44:15-16, five dialects, phonetic forms [mono:?], [salo:n], [taye:n], [tido:a]) states 'in all Rejang dialects the accent falls on the final syllabic vowel of the word'; McGinn 2009 (PL 601:412,416,418) repeats ultimate stress; Aichele 1984 (PL D-58:148) calls the last syllable the stressed one. Nothing found contradicts fixed final, weight-blind stress. Refinement from McGinn 2005 worth adding to the primary-stress rule/caution: the accent targets the final SYLLABIC vowel (final vowel sequences like -oa in [tido

sources.quote: p.15: 'Although it is not always obvious, in all Rejang dialects the accent falls on the final syllabic vowel of the word. The placement of the accent depends on syllable structure, and in particular on the prior identification of syllabic and nonsyllabic vowels (see section 4).' p.16: 'morphemes like daw ... and oa? ... are monosyllabic and hence in metrical terms bear no word-level accent ... umaa? [?umo:a?] 'home' and tidoa [tido:a] 'sleep' are disyllabic, with the accent falling on the second (final) syllabic vowel, as expected. Finally, canonical CVCVC morphs receive the accent on the fin
